medical.title: Artificial protein activates faulty insulin receptors and lowers blood sugar in mice
medical.summary: The body relies on a finely tuned network of receptors that unlock their docking sites in response to specific chemical signals. In some genetic diseases, however, mutations can leave these receptors unable to do their job. A recent study published in Science Translational Medicine has offered a way around this problem with an artificial protein designed to activate one such mutated receptor.

medical.title: mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute
medical.summary: Trials of an experimental Ebola vaccine aimed at the strain behind the current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have begun in neighboring Uganda, its virus research institute said Friday.

medical.title: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
medical.summary: For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

medical.title: A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes
medical.summary: In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins.

medical.title: Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism
medical.summary: For many people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ordinary sensory experiences can be unusually intense or overwhelming. A light touch or a mildly uncomfortable sensation may provoke a disproportionately strong response, making everyday activities difficult.

medical.title: Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
medical.summary: People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

medical.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
medical.summary: Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

medical.title: Does drinking raw milk actually deliver extra health benefits? Here's the science
medical.summary: The popularity of raw milk in Google searches and Instagram post topics has soared over the past 10 years, spurred on by influencers claiming there are benefits to consuming raw milk.

medical.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be due to your blood sugar and genes
medical.summary: Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

medical.title: Should you correct a friend's health myth? Ask yourself this question first
medical.summary: "You must drink eight glasses of water a day" is the kind of advice a friend might offer. But what the advice leaves out is that our daily fluid intake comes from a variety of sources, including other drinks and food.

medical.title: Liver protein as a potential biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
medical.summary: A key factor in identifying a biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) is understanding whether there are biological differences between treatment-resistant and non-treatment-resistant patients. Approximately 25% of all schizophrenia patients do not respond to medication. To better treat these patients, scientists at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry (MPIP) collected comprehensive data on cell distributions and proteins from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples taken from patients with and without TRS. When they compared these concentrations with those in the blood, they found elevated levels of the protein albumin in the CSF.

medical.title: Dreaming of better sleep? Personalized mathematical modeling may help turn that dream into reality
medical.summary: It's something we're all familiar with—the frustration of a bad night's sleep. But what is a bad night's sleep, exactly? For some, it might look like lying awake, being unable to fall asleep. For others, sleep may come quickly, only to be interrupted by unwanted early-morning wake-ups.

medical.title: How to recognize when video gaming becomes an addiction
medical.summary: Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

medical.title: Existing drug helps mice clear blood through meningeal lymphatic system after stroke
medical.summary: A drug already used to improve blood circulation and prevent certain types of stroke could have an unexpected new role in promoting recovery after bleeding in the brain. In a study published in Stroke, a team led by researchers at National Taiwan University found that cilostazol helped mice recover from intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) by boosting the brain's natural drainage system.

medical.title: Living wound patch pairs viruses and probiotics to fight resistant bacteria
medical.summary: Antibiotic-resistant germs are one of the greatest threats to our health. As the existing arsenal of antibiotics loses its effectiveness, even routine treatments can become considerably more risky. This "silent pandemic" is exacerbated by the ability of microorganisms to form biofilms. These extremely tenacious accumulations of germs can become a particular problem in hospitals. Antibiotics and disinfectants can hardly penetrate these films. In addition, biofilms promote the further spread of antibiotic resistance to other bacteria.

medical.title: Learning a new movement may start with a reusable pattern
medical.summary: A signature can remain recognizable when someone writes it with their non-dominant other hand, even though different muscles have produced it. Such flexibility hints at an internal pattern for an action that can be reused in different circumstances. But does that pattern emerge only after years of practice, or can it help us learn from the start?

medical.title: The littlest and cutest research subjects help explain infant brains
medical.summary: Every new parent knows the difficulty of trying to get a newborn to sleep. Northeastern University researchers have an added challenge: getting a newborn to sleep during a brain scan.

medical.title: What do puberty's wild hormone swings mean for teenage girls' mental health?
medical.summary: Behind the stereotype of the moody teenager is a far more complex picture: fluctuating hormones, emotional swings and a brain in the middle of major renovations.

medical.title: Brain's myelin 'brake' may hold clues to mental health disorders
medical.summary: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers have identified a cellular "brake" that helps prevent excessive myelin growth in the brain, which has been linked to mental health conditions such as major depressive disorder, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

medical.title: Aged care move disrupts regular health care
medical.summary: Moving into residential aged care can disrupt long-standing relationships with doctors and other health care providers, highlighting the need for stronger handover processes to protect continuity of care for older Australians, experts say.

medical.title: Why can't the heart repair itself? Study reveals a fundamental trade-off between beating and regeneration
medical.summary: The human heart beats more than 100,000 times a day, tirelessly pumping blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Yet despite its remarkable endurance, the heart has a major limitation: It has almost no capacity to repair itself after injury. A new study led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) helps explain why.

medical.title: Engineering antibiotics could expand the pool of new drug candidates
medical.summary: As more strains of dangerous bacteria become resistant to existing antibiotics, the quest to find new drugs has become more urgent. In hopes of expanding the pool of antibiotic candidates, MIT researchers have found a way to significantly improve the safety profile of drugs with antimicrobial activity that had previously been discarded.

medical.title: One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk
medical.summary: A massive study has revealed that exercising for pleasure and performing physical labor at work may have surprisingly different implications for brain health. While recreational exercise was linked to a 24% lower dementia risk, physically demanding work was associated with a 20% higher risk, suggesting that the context of movement matters.

medical.title: A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar
medical.summary: Texas A&M researchers have discovered a way to dramatically reduce the cost of a key component in an experimental injectable glucose sensor without sacrificing performance. The technology uses fluorescent light to measure glucose levels from beneath the skin.

medical.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
medical.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

science.title: New educational program developed for an often-overlooked group of gifted children
science.summary: Pupils from families with a lower socio-economic status (SES) perform less well at school than children from families with a high socio-economic status. They are also less likely to be identified as gifted pupils. Ph.D. candidate Lineke van Tricht has developed a program for schools to help pupils with a low SES make the most of their talents. "This is important for the young people themselves, but also for society as a whole," says Van Tricht, who will defend her thesis at Radboud University on 8 December 2026.

science.title: How mammals zigzagged their way to modern posture
science.summary: This is the story of how mammals came to dominate the Earth—and the crooked evolutionary path they trod en route. Early mammals and their ancestors left behind fossilized bones, footprints and lots of questions about how they moved. One key element of their evolutionary saga involved how these four-legged creatures shifted from what researchers call a "sprawled" stance, with limbs splayed like lizards, to more "erect" postures, with limbs directly beneath the body, that allowed for more speed and agility.

science.title: ATLAS finds hints of the hidden structure of the vacuum
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Bonn, together with colleagues from Oxford and Prague, played a leading role in analyzing particle collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The ATLAS Collaboration observed more proton collisions with the particle pattern it was looking for than expected. This could point to a phenomenon predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics that has never been directly observed, known as QCD instanton processes.

science.title: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades
science.summary: In contrast to the 2025 seasonal ozone hole above Antarctica, which was the fifth smallest since 1992, this year's ozone hole ranks as one of the largest in 48 years, based on long-term atmospheric observations, including data from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite. While this may sound alarming, it is important to remember that the size of the ozone hole varies naturally from year to year, and the long-term recovery of the ozone layer remains on track.

science.title: As families gather for Thanksgiving, college science students need training to talk across societal divides
science.summary: Most Americans have seen it happen. Relatives argue online about whether vaccines are safe and effective. Friends and neighbors trade jabs over climate change and whether anything should be done about it. Public officials and scientists disagree, loudly, about what causes autism or which vaccines children should get and when. No one gives an inch, and the rifts rarely heal. This Thanksgiving, after a contentious election season, many of those conversations will happen face to face around the dinner table.

science.title: Researchers develop mathematical model to estimate age and degradation of lunar impact craters
science.summary: Researchers from the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) and their collaborators have developed a mathematical model that uses morphometric parameters to rapidly estimate the degradation state and age of lunar impact craters. They applied the model to 140 impact craters in the Chang'e-6 landing area.

science.title: New fern species discovered after nearly 200 years of being mistaken for another
science.summary: Chinese researchers have formally described a new fern species that has been hiding in plain sight for nearly 200 years. Named Drynaria lineatisora, the species was collected as early as the 19th century in Myanmar and Vietnam, but it was repeatedly misidentified as the widespread Drynaria coronans. Recent field studies by researchers from the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden (XTBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and their collaborators confirmed that it is indeed a distinct species.

science.title: Ancient skull reveals an early relative of the largest bone-cracking hyena
science.summary: A newly identified prehistoric hyena from the northeastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau aids in the quest to trace the origin of a lion-sized bone crusher. Its partial skull also records a remarkable recovery: The animal lost a canine tooth and survived long enough for bone to fill the socket.

science.title: Why does the word 'huge' sound so large?
science.summary: "Meow!" "Woof!" "Moo!" "Baa!" The words we use to describe animal sounds are clearly inspired by the actual sounds the animals make.

science.title: The dark matter puzzle deepens: Nearby galaxies challenge cosmic simulations
science.summary: Galaxies appear to hold a surprise beneath their visible stars: Their inner regions contain less dark matter than some of our most advanced simulations predict. Dark matter is invisible, but its gravitational pull helps govern the motions of stars and gas. By measuring these movements, astronomers can reconstruct where this unseen matter lies and test the computer simulations used to understand the universe. A study of 136 nearby galaxies, involving the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), reveals a discrepancy that becomes more extensive in more massive systems, offering fresh clues about how galaxies form and evolve.

science.title: Researchers reveal sex chromosome evolution and molecular sex markers in the pitcher plant Nepenthes mirabilis
science.summary: Researchers have uncovered the genomic basis of sex determination in Nepenthes mirabilis, the only pitcher plant native to China, identifying an XX/XY sex chromosome system and molecular markers that can distinguish male from female plants long before they flower.

science.title: Dolly Parton gets a deep-sea namesake: Bathyadmetella dollypartonae
science.summary: A "beautiful" new species from one of the least-known areas of the ocean has been named after Dolly Parton. Scientists at the Natural History Museum work 9 to 5, and more besides, to name dozens of marine species every year. So, when they identified a new species of worm covered in pale, hairlike sheaths, there was only one choice for whom to name it after—and it wasn't Jolene.

science.title: Lizards build complex teeth differently from humans
science.summary: Researchers from the Institute of Biotechnology, part of the Helsinki Institute of Life Science (HiLIFE) at the University of Helsinki, have shown how evolution can produce similarly complex tooth shapes through very different biological mechanisms.

science.title: Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
science.summary: Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.

science.title: Meteor blast scars hint at Venus's gradual volcanic makeover
science.summary: In a radar image from NASA's Magellan spacecraft, a dark spot about 20 kilometers (12 miles) wide sits inside two bright halos on Venus (see images C and D above). The fainter outer halo spans some 180 kilometers (110 miles), yet there is no obvious crater at the center. A space rock may have created the entire pattern by exploding in the planet's thick atmosphere.

science.title: 3D modeling questions Viking 'fast fashion'
science.summary: High-resolution 3D modeling of Viking brooches and the molds used to make them identifies surprisingly few matches between them, indicating the brooches were not mass-produced, as previously thought, but instead made by individual, creative artisans.

science.title: Raman spectroscopy meets the sugar shack
science.summary: Tasting 250 maple syrup samples a day for six months can tire the palate of even the best-trained taster. But that's the job of the inspectors who sample about half of the 400,000 barrels graded every year by the Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ). This step, however, slows down the entire marketing chain.

science.title: Could a hidden planet twice Earth's mass explain strange orbits beyond Neptune?
science.summary: In the cold, dark Kuiper belt region beyond Neptune, some icy bodies travel on steeply tilted paths, while others stay far from the giant planets even at their closest approach to the sun. A simulation study suggests that a hidden planet about twice Earth's mass could help explain both populations of objects.

science.title: Familiar faces help children develop emotional understanding
science.summary: Across two studies, researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Queensland and Victoria University of Wellington studied parents' and children's recognition of emotional expressions.

science.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
science.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

science.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
science.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel

The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: How mammals zigzagged their way to modern posture
mix_items.summary: This is the story of how mammals came to dominate the Earth—and the crooked evolutionary path they trod en route. Early mammals and their ancestors left behind fossilized bones, footprints and lots of questions about how they moved. One key element of their evolutionary saga involved how these four-legged creatures shifted from what researchers call a "sprawled" stance, with limbs splayed like lizards, to more "erect" postures, with limbs directly beneath the body, that allowed for more speed and agility.

mix_items.title: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
mix_items.summary: For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

mix_items.summary: Fundația Motivation România se numără printre organizațiile care au contribuit la dezvoltarea Responsible Wheelchair Donation Toolkit, un ghid realizat de International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP), care promovează practici responsabile și sustenabile în donarea de scaune rulante, la nivel internațional. mix_items.title: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades
mix_items.summary: In contrast to the 2025 seasonal ozone hole above Antarctica, which was the fifth smallest since 1992, this year's ozone hole ranks as one of the largest in 48 years, based on long-term atmospheric observations, including data from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite. While this may sound alarming, it is important to remember that the size of the ozone hole varies naturally from year to year, and the long-term recovery of the ozone layer remains on track.

mix_items.title: “Școala în care ne simțim bine”
mix_items.summary: Ghid antibullying cu activități testate de mii de copii și 43 de ONG-uri. Articolul “Școala în care ne simțim bine” apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes
mix_items.summary: In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins.

mix_items.title: Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism
mix_items.summary: For many people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ordinary sensory experiences can be unusually intense or overwhelming. A light touch or a mildly uncomfortable sensation may provoke a disproportionately strong response, making everyday activities difficult.

mix_items.title: As families gather for Thanksgiving, college science students need training to talk across societal divides
mix_items.summary: Most Americans have seen it happen. Relatives argue online about whether vaccines are safe and effective. Friends and neighbors trade jabs over climate change and whether anything should be done about it. Public officials and scientists disagree, loudly, about what causes autism or which vaccines children should get and when. No one gives an inch, and the rifts rarely heal. This Thanksgiving, after a contentious election season, many of those conversations will happen face to face around the dinner table.

mix_items.title: Researchers develop mathematical model to estimate age and degradation of lunar impact craters
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) and their collaborators have developed a mathematical model that uses morphometric parameters to rapidly estimate the degradation state and age of lunar impact craters. They applied the model to 140 impact craters in the Chang'e-6 landing area.

mix_items.title: New fern species discovered after nearly 200 years of being mistaken for another
mix_items.summary: Chinese researchers have formally described a new fern species that has been hiding in plain sight for nearly 200 years. Named Drynaria lineatisora, the species was collected as early as the 19th century in Myanmar and Vietnam, but it was repeatedly misidentified as the widespread Drynaria coronans. Recent field studies by researchers from the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden (XTBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and their collaborators confirmed that it is indeed a distinct species.

mix_items.title: Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
mix_items.summary: People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

mix_items.title: Ancient skull reveals an early relative of the largest bone-cracking hyena
mix_items.summary: A newly identified prehistoric hyena from the northeastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau aids in the quest to trace the origin of a lion-sized bone crusher. Its partial skull also records a remarkable recovery: The animal lost a canine tooth and survived long enough for bone to fill the socket.

mix_items.title: Why does the word 'huge' sound so large?
mix_items.summary: "Meow!" "Woof!" "Moo!" "Baa!" The words we use to describe animal sounds are clearly inspired by the actual sounds the animals make.

mix_items.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
mix_items.summary: Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

mix_items.title: The dark matter puzzle deepens: Nearby galaxies challenge cosmic simulations
mix_items.summary: Galaxies appear to hold a surprise beneath their visible stars: Their inner regions contain less dark matter than some of our most advanced simulations predict. Dark matter is invisible, but its gravitational pull helps govern the motions of stars and gas. By measuring these movements, astronomers can reconstruct where this unseen matter lies and test the computer simulations used to understand the universe. A study of 136 nearby galaxies, involving the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), reveals a discrepancy that becomes more extensive in more massive systems, offering fresh clues about how galaxies form and evolve.

mix_items.title: Researchers reveal sex chromosome evolution and molecular sex markers in the pitcher plant Nepenthes mirabilis
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered the genomic basis of sex determination in Nepenthes mirabilis, the only pitcher plant native to China, identifying an XX/XY sex chromosome system and molecular markers that can distinguish male from female plants long before they flower.

mix_items.title: Does drinking raw milk actually deliver extra health benefits? Here's the science
mix_items.summary: The popularity of raw milk in Google searches and Instagram post topics has soared over the past 10 years, spurred on by influencers claiming there are benefits to consuming raw milk.

mix_items.title: Dolly Parton gets a deep-sea namesake: Bathyadmetella dollypartonae
mix_items.summary: A "beautiful" new species from one of the least-known areas of the ocean has been named after Dolly Parton. Scientists at the Natural History Museum work 9 to 5, and more besides, to name dozens of marine species every year. So, when they identified a new species of worm covered in pale, hairlike sheaths, there was only one choice for whom to name it after—and it wasn't Jolene.

mix_items.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be due to your blood sugar and genes
mix_items.summary: Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

mix_items.title: Lizards build complex teeth differently from humans
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Institute of Biotechnology, part of the Helsinki Institute of Life Science (HiLIFE) at the University of Helsinki, have shown how evolution can produce similarly complex tooth shapes through very different biological mechanisms.

mix_items.title: Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
mix_items.summary: Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.

mix_items.title: Should you correct a friend's health myth? Ask yourself this question first
mix_items.summary: "You must drink eight glasses of water a day" is the kind of advice a friend might offer. But what the advice leaves out is that our daily fluid intake comes from a variety of sources, including other drinks and food.

mix_items.title: Meteor blast scars hint at Venus's gradual volcanic makeover
mix_items.summary: In a radar image from NASA's Magellan spacecraft, a dark spot about 20 kilometers (12 miles) wide sits inside two bright halos on Venus (see images C and D above). The fainter outer halo spans some 180 kilometers (110 miles), yet there is no obvious crater at the center. A space rock may have created the entire pattern by exploding in the planet's thick atmosphere.

mix_items.title: Liver protein as a potential biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
mix_items.summary: A key factor in identifying a biomarker for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) is understanding whether there are biological differences between treatment-resistant and non-treatment-resistant patients. Approximately 25% of all schizophrenia patients do not respond to medication. To better treat these patients, scientists at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry (MPIP) collected comprehensive data on cell distributions and proteins from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples taken from patients with and without TRS. When they compared these concentrations with those in the blood, they found elevated levels of the protein albumin in the CSF.

mix_items.title: Dreaming of better sleep? Personalized mathematical modeling may help turn that dream into reality
mix_items.summary: It's something we're all familiar with—the frustration of a bad night's sleep. But what is a bad night's sleep, exactly? For some, it might look like lying awake, being unable to fall asleep. For others, sleep may come quickly, only to be interrupted by unwanted early-morning wake-ups.

mix_items.title: 3D modeling questions Viking 'fast fashion'
mix_items.summary: High-resolution 3D modeling of Viking brooches and the molds used to make them identifies surprisingly few matches between them, indicating the brooches were not mass-produced, as previously thought, but instead made by individual, creative artisans.

mix_items.title: How to recognize when video gaming becomes an addiction
mix_items.summary: Most people who play video games can spend hours enjoying them without experiencing any problems. But for a small minority, gaming becomes so important that relationships, education or work begin to suffer. How can we tell when enthusiasm has become a disorder?

mix_items.title: Raman spectroscopy meets the sugar shack
mix_items.summary: Tasting 250 maple syrup samples a day for six months can tire the palate of even the best-trained taster. But that's the job of the inspectors who sample about half of the 400,000 barrels graded every year by the Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ). This step, however, slows down the entire marketing chain.

mix_items.title: Could a hidden planet twice Earth's mass explain strange orbits beyond Neptune?
mix_items.summary: In the cold, dark Kuiper belt region beyond Neptune, some icy bodies travel on steeply tilted paths, while others stay far from the giant planets even at their closest approach to the sun. A simulation study suggests that a hidden planet about twice Earth's mass could help explain both populations of objects.

mix_items.title: Familiar faces help children develop emotional understanding
mix_items.summary: Across two studies, researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Queensland and Victoria University of Wellington studied parents' and children's recognition of emotional expressions.

mix_items.title: Existing drug helps mice clear blood through meningeal lymphatic system after stroke
mix_items.summary: A drug already used to improve blood circulation and prevent certain types of stroke could have an unexpected new role in promoting recovery after bleeding in the brain. In a study published in Stroke, a team led by researchers at National Taiwan University found that cilostazol helped mice recover from intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) by boosting the brain's natural drainage system.

mix_items.title: Living wound patch pairs viruses and probiotics to fight resistant bacteria
mix_items.summary: Antibiotic-resistant germs are one of the greatest threats to our health. As the existing arsenal of antibiotics loses its effectiveness, even routine treatments can become considerably more risky. This "silent pandemic" is exacerbated by the ability of microorganisms to form biofilms. These extremely tenacious accumulations of germs can become a particular problem in hospitals. Antibiotics and disinfectants can hardly penetrate these films. In addition, biofilms promote the further spread of antibiotic resistance to other bacteria.

mix_items.title: Learning a new movement may start with a reusable pattern
mix_items.summary: A signature can remain recognizable when someone writes it with their non-dominant other hand, even though different muscles have produced it. Such flexibility hints at an internal pattern for an action that can be reused in different circumstances. But does that pattern emerge only after years of practice, or can it help us learn from the start?

mix_items.title: The littlest and cutest research subjects help explain infant brains
mix_items.summary: Every new parent knows the difficulty of trying to get a newborn to sleep. Northeastern University researchers have an added challenge: getting a newborn to sleep during a brain scan.

mix_items.title: What do puberty's wild hormone swings mean for teenage girls' mental health?
mix_items.summary: Behind the stereotype of the moody teenager is a far more complex picture: fluctuating hormones, emotional swings and a brain in the middle of major renovations.

mix_items.title: Brain's myelin 'brake' may hold clues to mental health disorders
mix_items.summary: UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers have identified a cellular "brake" that helps prevent excessive myelin growth in the brain, which has been linked to mental health conditions such as major depressive disorder, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

mix_items.title: Aged care move disrupts regular health care
mix_items.summary: Moving into residential aged care can disrupt long-standing relationships with doctors and other health care providers, highlighting the need for stronger handover processes to protect continuity of care for older Australians, experts say.

mix_items.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
mix_items.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

mix_items.title: Why can't the heart repair itself? Study reveals a fundamental trade-off between beating and regeneration
mix_items.summary: The human heart beats more than 100,000 times a day, tirelessly pumping blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients throughout the body. Yet despite its remarkable endurance, the heart has a major limitation: It has almost no capacity to repair itself after injury. A new study led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) helps explain why.

mix_items.title: Engineering antibiotics could expand the pool of new drug candidates
mix_items.summary: As more strains of dangerous bacteria become resistant to existing antibiotics, the quest to find new drugs has become more urgent. In hopes of expanding the pool of antibiotic candidates, MIT researchers have found a way to significantly improve the safety profile of drugs with antimicrobial activity that had previously been discarded.

mix_items.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
mix_items.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

mix_items.title: One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk
mix_items.summary: A massive study has revealed that exercising for pleasure and performing physical labor at work may have surprisingly different implications for brain health. While recreational exercise was linked to a 24% lower dementia risk, physically demanding work was associated with a 20% higher risk, suggesting that the context of movement matters.

mix_items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. mix_items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. Between Nov. 13 and 16, nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, for the eighth International Marine Conservation […]

mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar
mix_items.summary: Texas A&M researchers have discovered a way to dramatically reduce the cost of a key component in an experimental injectable glucose sensor without sacrificing performance. The technology uses fluorescent light to measure glucose levels from beneath the skin.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
mix_items.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
